title: The dice
hook: Yudhishthira gambles a kingdom, then his brothers, then his wife

segments.voice: Yesterday: two sets of cousins, five and a hundred, one palace and one throne. Your line was one house. Did you say hello across a split? Day seventy-two.

Just one more hand. One more spin. One more episode, one more scroll, one more bet to win back what you lost on the last one. The Pandavas have done well. They've built a shining city of their own, Indraprastha, with a hall so magical that when Duryodhana visits, he mistakes a floor for a pool and a pool for a floor, and falls in, and people laugh. He goes home burning. His uncle Shakuni has an idea. Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, can't refuse a challenge. And Shakuni is a master of the dice.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `DURYODHANA FALLS IN THE POOL.` → `SHAKUNI, MASTER OF THE DICE.`

segments.voice: The invitation comes: a friendly game in the great hall at Hastinapura. Yudhishthira knows it's a trap. He says so. And he goes anyway, because a king of his kind doesn't refuse a challenge. The game begins. Shakuni throws for Duryodhana, and in the popular telling his dice are loaded; the text simply says he's a master of deceit at the game. Yudhishthira stakes a jewel and loses. Gold. Loses. Chariots. His army. His treasury. His whole kingdom. Each time, he's sure the next throw will turn it. Then Shakuni says: what else do you have? And Yudhishthira stakes his brothers. The twins first. Then Arjuna. Then Bhima. He loses every one. Then he stakes himself. And loses. The hall is silent. And Shakuni says: there's one stake you haven't played. Your wife. And Yudhishthira, the man known for never lying, the son of dharma himself, stakes Draupadi. And the dice fall. Vidura, the king's wise half-brother, has begged them all to stop the game, and no one listens. The other elders in the hall, the grandfather Bhishma, the teacher Drona, the blind king, let it go on. Look at who's throwing. Yudhishthira isn't a fool. He's the brother known for wisdom and honesty. And that's the frightening part. The dice didn't ruin him in one throw. They ruined him one reasonable-looking bet at a time, each one trying to fix the last. The hand keeps reaching, and at some point nobody, not even him, stops it. Tomorrow we'll see what happened to Draupadi in that hall. Today, just watch the hand.
screen: `HE KNOWS IT'S A TRAP. HE GOES.` · `JEWELS, ARMY, KINGDOM, GONE.` · `HIS BROTHERS. HIMSELF. HIS WIFE.` · `NOBODY STOPS THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest in your lap. Feel them there, still. Now think of a losing streak you kept betting on. Maybe not money. An argument you kept doubling down on. A relationship you kept pouring into. A habit you kept telling yourself you'd fix tomorrow. Notice the moment, each time, when the hand reached for the next throw. Then look at your hands now, resting. Still. You can stop them. That's all. The bell holds the time.
The dice. A rigged game, a wise man who couldn't stop, and a kingdom, four brothers and a wife lost one throw at a time.
Your line: stop the hand. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for one more, of anything, put your hand down for one breath first. Day seventy-two.

howItsDone: The dice game in the Sabha Parva is retold in homes, classical dance and theater, and readers often point to it as the moment the great war became hard to stop.

original.note: Sanskrit: dyuta, gambling with dice. The whole episode is called the dyuta.

trapdoor: what you thought: a foolish man gambles everything.
what it means: a wise man loses everything one reasonable-looking bet at a time, and nobody stops his hand.
what a scholar hears: dice games were part of old royal rituals, and Yudhishthira's refusal to decline a challenge follows the warrior code he held.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the hall at Indraprastha; Duryodhana's fall; the dice game, the dyuta)

notes: Duryodhana's fall in the maya-hall: the popular telling adds Draupadi laughing ('the son of a blind man is blind'); the script only says 'people laugh' because the attribution to Draupadi is disputed. Confirm.
Loaded dice: the text calls Shakuni a master of deceit at dice; loaded dice (sometimes made from his father's bones) are later popular tellings. Confirm framing.
The order of stakes (twins, Arjuna, Bhima, himself, Draupadi) follows the Sabha Parva as remembered; confirm.

Review edit: the earlier draft said the elders 'sat there and did nothing'; in the Sabha Parva Vidura protests strongly and urges the game be stopped, so the script now names him. Bhishma's and Drona's silence is mainly about Draupadi's question (tomorrow); confirm the wording here.
Trapdoor: dice in royal ritual (the rajasuya includes a ritual dice game); confirm the wording.

Editor review (days 57–75): hook no longer tells the listener what they've seen or felt; cut the uncounted 'a thousand chariots' and the superlative 'the wisest of the brothers'; 'can't lose at dice' softened to 'a master of the dice' to match the text; softened the howItsDone claims.
